Nestlé S.A. (NESN-CH) · Investment memo · 19 November 2026

Nestlé: the operating engine is working, but a shrinking perimeter holds reported EPS flat for two years, so estimates will fall before they rise

Written 19 November 2026 at a share price of CHF 88.01, the 16 November 2026 price used in the Financial Analyst's model (update 1), which is the source of all forecasts.

How to read the numbers

  • Margin is the underlying trading operating profit (UTOP) margin. EPS is underlying EPS on the brokers' basis. RIG (real internal growth) is Nestlé's measure of growth in volume and mix.
  • Consensus is the FactSet median of 16 November 2026. Company-compiled consensus is Nestlé's own collection of 9 October 2026, made before the Q3 sales update and before Russia left the accounts.
  • The engine is EPS growth at constant currency on a constant perimeter. The wrapper is everything around the engine that moves reported EPS: Russia's exit, the disposals, the franc, finance costs and the absence of buybacks.
  • Latest data. The last profit, margin and cash figures are for the half to June 2026; the Q3 update of 22 October 2026 gave sales only. The next results are the FY26 results on 18 February 2027. End note 3 lists three model lines that should not be quoted as printed.

#0Summary: summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one line. Nestlé is a good engine inside a shrinking wrapper, and today's share price already pays for the engine.

The verdict for Richard: the skew is not unusually positive today, so follow the shares closely rather than buy now.

Consensus EPS is more likely to be cut than raised over the next six to twelve months, for mechanical reasons. The estimate reset of February to April 2027 could clear the way for a positive skew. A lower entry price would do the same work faster: a 15% return over 18 months needs an entry price of about CHF 84 (#12).

  1. The engine is working, and the engine is the predictable part of the case. RIG has risen for three quarters, to 2.8% in Q3 2026. Savings are running ahead of plan. Coffee and cocoa costs are falling into 2027. New petcare capacity is filling. At constant currency and on a constant perimeter, EPS grows about 5% a year. On the engine I agree with the market.
  2. The wrapper holds reported EPS flat for two years. Russia has left the accounts, and the low-margin businesses being sold, about 6% of sales, leave in 2027. The model also assumes that the franc keeps drifting stronger, that finance costs do not fall and that there are no buybacks. The model's EPS is CHF 4.55 for FY26 and CHF 4.58 for FY28: 4% below consensus for FY27 and 9% below for FY28.
  3. The gap to consensus is my main difference from the market, and the gap is mostly arithmetic, not opinion. About three-quarters of the FY27 gap is Russia and the exits. Nestlé has published those figures, but the consensus median has not yet removed them. The brokers who have rebuilt their models for Russia already sit close to the model.
  4. Consensus estimates will therefore fall before they rise. I expect FY27 consensus EPS to move from CHF 4.72 to about CHF 4.60 by mid-2027, mostly between February and April. Falling estimates are the opposite of the skew Richard looks for. Nestlé will probably meet its guidance throughout, because it guides in organic growth, margin and cash, measures that the wrapper barely touches.
  5. The drag from the wrapper is finite and dated, which is what makes the case worth following. The perimeter stops shrinking during 2028, and FY29 is the first clean year. Three things outside the model would each help: a franc that stays at today's rate, a second savings programme, and any step on capital returns. The estimate reset of early 2027 could be the clearing event after which the skew turns positive.
  6. The valuation is fuller than the screens show. On consensus earnings the shares are on 17.6 times two-year-forward earnings; on the model's earnings they are on 19.3 times. The guideline fair multiple is 20.17 times, so only 4.5% of re-rating is left on the model's numbers.
  7. The return is mostly dividend. The model's total return to its 18-month column is +16.2%: 7.2 points from dividends, 4.5 from the multiple and 4.3 from earnings. I regard the dividend as dependable, the earnings part as back-loaded and the multiple as the least secure part, so I plan on +7% to +12%.
  8. The share price follows the variable that matters least to EPS. The shares have re-rated on quarterly RIG, yet a full point of RIG is worth only about 1.4% of EPS. The franc, the perimeter and the price-cost spread on coffee and cocoa move EPS far more, and the market has so far looked through all three.
  9. For a holder who does not measure returns in francs, the franc is mostly noise. Almost none of Nestlé's profit is earned in francs, but the shares are priced in francs. A stronger franc cuts franc EPS and raises the value of the shares in the holder's own currency by a similar amount (#1).

#1Strong/improving tailwinds in the operating environment; and an absence of headwinds/risks

Conclusion: The environment is a modest net headwind with a one-year commodity window inside it, so it supports FY27 margins but will not by itself produce upgrades.

Evidence

  • Demand has switched from price to volume. RIG has risen for three quarters, to 2.8% in Q3 2026, and was positive in every zone in Q3. Pricing has fallen from 2.8% in FY25 to 1.1% in Q3, and to 0.2% in Europe. About 0.2 to 0.3 points of Q3 RIG came from a heatwave in Waters and from shipment timing in confectionery.
  • Input costs are falling, for now. Green coffee is about 5% of Nestlé's sales and cocoa about 1%. Jefferies has coffee costs down about 20% in 2026 and 11% in 2027. Morgan Stanley's measure of chocolate makers' pipeline costs falls 48% in H1-27 and then rises 3% in H2-27. Freight, milk and energy costs are rising, and a strong El Niño is forecast into early 2027.
  • Retailers will claim part of the cost relief. Private label holds 29% of European coffee, and more than 40% of value in Spain and the UK. Retailers' buying alliances now delist brands across borders: Intermarché dropped about 30 Nestlé brands in early 2026.
  • The franc has cut reported sales every year: by 7.8%, 3.7% and 5.7% in 2023 to 2025, and by 3.7% in the first nine months of 2026. Q3 2026 was the first quarter in years in which the currency effect was favourable.
  • Slow structural drags persist. Use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among US adults rose from 3% to 11% between 2024 and 2026, and births in China fell 17% in 2025.
  • Emerging markets and digital channels are the structural positive. Zone Asia, Oceania and Africa grew 6.4% in Q3, with RIG of 5.0%. E-commerce is 21.6% of sales and grew 15.3%.
  • The sector has been re-rated by rotation, not by earnings. European staples rose 12%, to 17 times forward earnings, in October as money left cyclical shares (Morgan Stanley).

Inference. The tailwinds are cyclical and dated; the headwinds are structural and slow. The commodity benefit has a window that runs roughly from H2-26 to Q3-27.

Within the commodity window, the order of events creates a double squeeze that brokers describe in halves but rarely join up. Private-label suppliers reprice within three to six months, while Nestlé's commodity cover runs longer. Retailers will therefore press Nestlé to cut prices in the European negotiating round of early 2027, before Nestlé's own costs have fully fallen. If coffee and cocoa costs turn up again in H2-27, Nestlé will have conceded price just before it pays more.

So what. FY27 is the best year of the cycle for the spread between price and cost, and FY28 gives some of that gain back. Over 18 months the environment roughly cancels out, and after that it leans against Nestlé. The environment therefore does not carry the case; the company's own actions must.

A reframing of the franc that I think is under-used. Only about 1% of Nestlé's sales is in francs, but the shares are priced in francs. A stronger franc lowers franc EPS. For a holder who measures returns in sterling, euros or dollars, a stronger franc also raises the value of each franc of share price, by about the same amount. The franc is therefore a real drag on reported growth, on estimate revisions and on dividend cover, but mostly not a drag on that holder's economic return. This inference is my own; the broker material does not make it.

Against the market. I agree with the market that the volume turn is real and broad. I differ in two places. The market treats falling coffee and cocoa costs as a margin gain to be banked; I treat about half of the gain as given back to retailers and the rest as temporary. Most brokers also hold the franc at today's rate, whereas the model assumes that it drifts stronger.

Strongest counter-case. The commodity window may be longer and richer than I allow. Futures curves for coffee and cocoa slope down through 2028, and the industry holds more than ten months of cocoa cover. Only about 5% of Nestlé's sales is roast and ground coffee, the format in which shelf prices track bean costs most closely. Soluble coffee and capsules, sold partly direct to the consumer, keep more of any relief.

What would change my view. More positive: the European round settles by March 2027 without multi-country delistings, and the H2-26 gross margin prints near 47%. More negative: arabica and cocoa futures up 20% or more by mid-2027, or European pricing below −1%.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Volume has turned broadly (RIG up to 2.8% in Q3, positive in every zone; Asia-Oceania-Africa RIG 5.0%, e-commerce +15%), but the coffee and cocoa relief is a dated window to about Q3-27 that European retailers will claim part of in the early-2027 round, and the structural drags (concentrated buying alliances and delistings, private label, GLP-1, China births, a franc that trims reported growth) persist, so the environment is a modest net headwind over two to three years. Consensus sales growth at the 17th percentile fits that; I agree with the External change forces group (43) and place it just below Kerry's neutral environment and just above Carlsberg's mature one.

#2Strong/improving internally-driven corporate change forces; and an absence of problems/risks

Conclusion: Internal change is strong, broad and well executed, but it is self-funded and largely reinvested, so it secures the volume recovery more than it lifts EPS.

Evidence

  • Leadership has changed at every level. Philipp Navratil became chief executive in September 2025, the third in 13 months. Pablo Isla, formerly of Inditex, is the first outsider to chair the board, and the board is fully independent. The chief financial officer, Anna Manz, now also runs mergers and acquisitions.
  • The strategy is coherent and measurable. Volume comes before price. There are four core categories. Advertising is concentrated on 135 to 150 brands, down from more than 400. Growth platforms have been widened from 10% to 30% of sales. Five zones have become three. A minimum level of RIG now gates the annual bonus.
  • The cost programme is large and ahead of plan. Fuel for Growth targets CHF 3.0bn of gross savings by end-2027, about 3.4% of sales. It delivered CHF 1.1bn in FY25 against CHF 0.7bn planned, and CHF 1.7bn cumulatively by June 2026. It removes 16,000 roles, about 6% of the workforce.
  • The money is being spent on volume. Advertising has risen from 8.1% to 8.9% of sales, and Nestlé is investing an extra CHF 600m in the growth platforms in 2026.
  • The perimeter is shrinking by about 8% of sales (table below). Waters, mainstream vitamins and the remaining ice cream business are leaving. Russia left the accounts at end-September 2026, after it was placed under external administration.
  • A supply constraint has gone. The pet food plant at Batavia, Ohio opened in August 2026. Petcare RIG was 4.3% in Q3, with shipments to retailers matching sales to shoppers.

Inference. Nestlé is running the most comprehensive change programme in its modern history, with unusual speed and candour. The change programme is the strongest part of the case.

One pot of savings is doing two jobs, however: it funds the volume recovery, and it is also meant to rebuild the margin. I estimate that about a quarter of the CHF 3.0bn, roughly CHF 0.7bn or 80bp of margin, shows in the margin by FY28. The rest pays for ordinary cost inflation, advertising and price restraint. Peers show the same split: Danone kept 18bp of a 77bp operating improvement in 2025, and Colgate's 290bp of savings in Q3-26 almost exactly matched 300bp of input inflation.

The change programme leaves the balance sheet untouched: leverage, the dividend and the stake in L'Oréal are unchanged. Nestlé owns about 20% of L'Oréal, a stake worth about CHF 42bn, or roughly 19% of Nestlé's own market value.

So what. Credit the volume recovery and the savings delivery in full. Withhold credit for a margin above about 16.6% to 16.8% until a reported half-year shows it.

Where a positive surprise could come from. Navratil has said there is "no ceiling" on savings, and the only targets Nestlé has raised under him are cost targets. I put the chance of a second or extended savings programme at about 35% by February 2027 and about 55% by February 2028; such a programme is the most likely form of any "raise". A second route is a restated margin ambition for the new perimeter. I would read a restated ambition as arithmetic, not as an upgrade: 17% on the new perimeter equals about 16.75% on the old one.

Negatives to track

  • Cutting 6% of staff in two years has no precedent at Nestlé. Most of the white-collar cuts land in 2027, and expert calls report talent leaving.
  • A 30bp pension credit flattered the H1-26 margin, and Nestlé disclosed the credit only when analysts asked.
  • Reported net income for FY26 will be about CHF 5.5bn to 6bn after Russia and other charges, against about CHF 11.7bn underlying. The low reported figure is a headline risk for February, not a cash problem.
  • Infant formula sales were still about 10% below their pre-recall level in mid-2026.

Against the market. The market knows these changes and prices them. I agree on their direction and strength, but differ on how much reaches EPS. Jefferies speaks of CHF 2bn of "net" savings; I see CHF 0.7bn in the margin, because cost inflation takes the difference.

Strongest counter-case. The failure mode is the path Kraft Heinz took. If Nestlé ever defends the margin or the dividend by cutting advertising, the volume recovery reverses and takes years to repair. Nestlé's bonus gate on RIG is designed to prevent that outcome.

What would change my view. More positive: a second savings programme with a stated net benefit. More negative: advertising below 8.9% of sales at the FY26 results, or Q1-27 RIG below about 1.5% once the lap of the recall is removed.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. The most complete reset in Nestlé's modern history is under way and ahead of plan: new CEO, outsider chair and independent board, a focused strategy with a RIG bonus gate, Fuel for Growth at CHF 1.7bn of CHF 3.0bn delivered by June 2026, Batavia capacity filling, and an 8% perimeter cut; but it repairs a mature business, is self-funded and largely reinvested (about CHF 0.7bn, 80bp, reaches the margin by FY28), the disposals proceeds repay debt rather than retire shares, and 6% staff cuts, the pension-credit flattering and the formula recall are internal problems still to clear. That is the complete repair-only programme the levels place in the low 60s, coherent with the Internal change forces group (65), above Odfjell's incremental self-help and just below OEM's change of control already showing in record results.

#3A value chain and industry structure that is favourable; a business model with competitive advantage and barriers to entry; an above average or better financial profile; a dynamic management team with stretching goals, the right strategy and winning culture

Conclusion: Nestlé has a strong franchise in its profit core, with above-average margins and cash generation, held back by a contested middle, the highest leverage in its peer group and a passive approach to capital.

Evidence

  • Positions. Nestlé is number one or two where it earns most. It leads global coffee. In petcare, Purina has 30% of the global market against 33% for Mars, and the two hold about half of US retail. Nestlé is among the leaders in infant formula and medical nutrition. Petcare and premium coffee are an estimated 55% to 60% of operating profit.
  • Value chain. Brand owners keep the richest margin in the food value chain: Nestlé's gross margin is about 46% and its operating margin about 16%, while processors earn 2% to 5% and grocers 3% to 6%. Suppliers are fragmented. Retailers are concentrated and getting stronger.
  • Market share. Nestlé says it lost share for years through 18 underperforming business cells. The rate of share loss has since fallen by about 60%.
  • Returns. Return on invested capital was 12.5% in FY25, against 19% at Unilever.
  • Balance sheet. Net debt was 2.85 times EBITDA at end-2025 on the company's definition, and 3.2 times on FactSet's definition, which includes leases. On FactSet's definition Nestlé is the most indebted of its peer set (chart below).
  • Cash. Free cash flow is CHF 9bn to 10bn a year, and capital spending has fallen below 5% of sales.
  • Management in action. In 14 months Navratil has doubled the savings target, named the job cuts publicly, struck three disposals and tied bonuses to volume. The board is among the strongest in European staples.
  • Capital allocation record. Nestlé funded the CHF 20bn buyback completed in 2024 with borrowed money, at an average of about CHF 107 a share, 21% above today's price. The acquisitions of 2019 to 2021 (Bountiful, Aimmune, Blue Bottle) were written down or sold.
  • Goals. Nestlé targets organic growth of 4% or more, RIG of at least 2% and a margin of 17% or more. These goals sit below Unilever's growth target of 4% to 6%, and below Nestlé's own margin aim of 17.5% to 18.5% set in 2017.

Inference. Nestlé is two businesses: a protected core of petcare, coffee systems, and medical and infant nutrition, which can grow 4% to 6%; and a contested middle of mainstream food, confectionery, developed-market instant coffee and US frozen food, which grows 0% to 2% only with price investment.

For the group as a whole, the binding constraint is the retailer, not the rival brand. The retailer's power is why Nestlé's pricing power amounts to cost pass-through, and why Nestlé has to buy volume with price investment (#5).

Nestlé's barriers to entry are strong, but its edge against existing rivals has weakened, as its returns and its market-share record show. The new management is a clear improvement in operating terms. Its goals restore a former standard rather than stretch beyond it, and its capital allocation is prudent but passive.

So what. The foundations support steady organic growth of 3.5% to 4% and a margin that rebuilds slowly. They do not support growth or returns above the peer group. Nestlé is a mature distributor of cash: about 90% of free cash flow after leases goes to the dividend.

Against the market. Redburn puts the shares at a 14% premium to European staples, against a ten-year average premium of 6%, and bears call that premium unmerited. My view is that the profit core deserves a premium and the group as a whole does not. The L'Oréal stake also flatters the headline multiple by about one turn: Deutsche Bank put the core at 16.4 times when the headline was 17.6 times.

Strongest counter-case. Scale and breadth are worth more than the returns show. Aggregate organic growth has stayed within 2% to 4% outside the inflation years. Compliance costs favour the largest player. Emerging markets, about 41% of sales, offer a long runway.

What would change my view. Sustained share gains in the 18 underperforming business cells; return on invested capital moving towards the mid-teens; any use of the balance sheet at a sensible price.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. A protected core (petcare, coffee systems, medical and infant nutrition, 60-70% of profit) sits in concentrated, high-barrier categories where Nestlé is number one or two, beside a contested middle facing private label and concentrated retailers with no real pricing power, years of share loss, ROIC of 11-12.5% (69th percentile; below Unilever's 19%) and gross margin at the 71st percentile, leverage of about 3x (highest in its peer set) and a poor capital allocation record under a promising but unproven new management. I sit above the groups' average (58/56/48/48) because the core's barriers, the low cyclicality and the predictability of 2-4% organic growth weigh more for a business as it is becoming after the exits; it belongs just below Carlsberg (number-one/two positions, best ROIC among brewers) and above Helios Towers.

#4Conservative current guidance; proactivity in keeping sell-side expectations conservative; a track record of fundamental delivery, raising guidance and raising sell-side estimates

Conclusion: Guidance is credible and likely to be met at every event, but it is not conservative where it matters for upgrades, and Nestlé's longer record is of estimates falling, not rising.

Evidence

  • FY26 guidance. Organic growth of 3% to 4%, against about 3.7% for the first nine months. A margin that improves on FY25's 16.1%, with the second half "broadly similar" to the first half's 16.4%. Free cash flow above CHF 9bn.
  • The record on guidance. FY24 guidance was cut twice, from about 4% organic growth to the 2.2% delivered. FY25 guidance was set low and met. FY26 guidance was narrowed, not raised, and its margin phasing was softened in July.
  • The record against estimates. Nestlé has beaten on the top line four times in a row, from Q4-25 to Q3-26. FY25 free cash flow was CHF 9.15bn against guidance of "at least CHF 8.0bn". But consensus EPS for each of FY26, FY27 and FY28 has fallen 8% to 11% from its peak, and Nestlé has walked its margin targets down since 2017.
  • How Nestlé manages expectations. It publishes an aide-mémoire before each event and compiles its own consensus. It has chosen not to quantify the effect of the exits until their closing dates are fixed, and will do so on 18 February 2027.

Inference. Nestlé's guidance today is honest and cautious, not sandbagged. The one cushion is in cash: the model has FY26 free cash flow of about CHF 9.85bn on the company's definition, against guidance of more than CHF 9bn, because the second half of 2025 alone produced CHF 6.8bn. There is no cushion on FY27 EPS, because Nestlé does not guide EPS.

The structural point is that Nestlé guides in measures the wrapper barely touches. Organic growth excludes currency and perimeter, and the low-margin exits help the margin percentage. Only free cash flow shows the wrapper. Nestlé can therefore meet its guidance at each of the six events in the next 18 months while reported EPS is flat and consensus EPS falls.

What I expect

  • FY26: all three guided lines met (about 90% likely), with cash beaten.
  • FY27 guidance on 18 February: organic growth of "3% to 4%", a margin "to improve" and free cash flow "above CHF 9bn". I put the chance of a guide in line with expectations at about 60%, better at 15% and worse at 25%. A repeat of "above CHF 9bn" would sit about 10% below the cash-flow consensus of CHF 10.2bn, because free cash flow is the one guided line where the perimeter shows.
  • Where guidance language could soften: in July 2027, on the second-half margin, and in February 2028, on FY28.
  • The medium-term ambition is not conservative. Organic growth of 4% or more with RIG of 2% implies pricing of about 2%; I expect 1% to 1.5%. The model reaches a 17% margin only in FY29.

So what. Any upside will show as quarterly sales beats, not as raised guidance. No stored conservatism is waiting to be released into EPS.

Against the market. The market reads the run of beats as evidence of conservative guidance. I read it as a low bar on sales and no bar at all on EPS.

Strongest counter-case. A chief executive who has raised only cost targets, and has beaten on sales and cash, may be building room on purpose. Nestlé could set the FY27 guide below a run-rate that then beats all year.

What would change my view. A FY27 guide with a floor on RIG above 2%; any guidance on EPS at constant currency; disclosure of net savings.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. FY24 guidance was cut twice (about 4% to 2.2%), FY25 was set low and met, FY26 narrowed not raised with the margin phasing softened, and while there have been four top-line beats and cash beats, consensus EPS for FY26-28 has fallen 8-11% from peak and margin targets have been walked down since 2017; current guidance is honest but not conservative where it matters, with nothing guiding FY27 EPS. Coherent with the Guidance (45) and Sell-side estimates (43) groups: just below Sdiptech's untested new targets, just above Instalco's recent miss of every target.

#5A business model that has pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out/cost control scope and/or reinforcing feedback loops, meaning revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth

Conclusion: Nestlé's business model has cost-out and a temporary price-cost gain but little true pricing power, modest operating leverage that is being reinvested, and no help from financial leverage, so profit grows only a little faster than sales.

Evidence, lever by lever

  • Pricing power is cost pass-through with a lag.
    • In 2022 and 2023, pricing of about 8% took RIG down to −0.3%.
    • In FY25, pricing of 2.8% still left the gross margin down 110bp.
    • A price rise of 8% on Starbucks at-home products cost 4% of volume.
    • Real pricing power exists in pockets: soluble coffee in emerging markets, Nespresso, Purina Pro Plan and medical nutrition.
  • Operating leverage is real but spent.
    • Truly fixed costs are about 25% to 30% of sales.
    • Advertising is held as a ratio to sales, so the margin on an extra unit of volume is about 22% to 27%.
    • Cost inflation on the fixed base absorbs most of that incremental margin: volume growth of 2% or more adds only 10bp to 15bp of margin a year.
    • In 2021, RIG of 5.5% came with a margin 30bp lower. Nestlé's margin follows the price-cost spread, not volume.
  • Financial leverage is neutral at best.
    • Interest cover is about ten times, and about 80% of debt is at fixed rates.
    • About 46% of debt refinances within five years, at about 4% against 2.3% today.
    • There are no buybacks. Over FY19 to FY24 a falling share count added about 2% a year to EPS.
  • Cost-out is large, and Nestlé keeps about a quarter of it (#2).
  • Feedback loops.
    • Two loops reinforce: volume funds advertising, which brings volume; and pet capacity brings share, which brings scale.
    • Three loops balance: retailers' claim on cost relief, the franc's effect on reported earnings, and the dividend's claim on cash.

Inference. Revenue growth does not turn into outsized profit growth at Nestlé today. Organic growth of about 3.6% becomes about 5% of EPS growth before the wrapper and about zero after it. The model's margin gain is about 20bp a year, half the 40bp a year of 2016 to 2020, when inflation was lower and advertising was flat.

The loops interact, and FY28 is the year of greatest strain. In FY28 the commodity relief ends, the savings programme has delivered its last tranche, and stranded central costs surface as service agreements with the divested businesses expire. The volume recovery must then fund itself. Because the dividend takes almost all free cash flow, a shock in FY28 would force a choice between advertising and the dividend.

So what. Do not expect leverage of any kind to amplify earnings before FY29. The spare lever is the cost base after 2027: distribution costs at 8.4% of sales, the long tail of brands, and the contested middle of the portfolio.

Against the market. Jefferies expects operating leverage from petcare and "net and genuine" savings to carry the margin to 17.0% in FY27. I think Nestlé recycles most of that gain into advertising and price. I side with Morgan Stanley on how little of the savings drops through to the margin, but against its view that market share losses continue.

Strongest counter-case. In 2016 to 2020, CHF 2.8bn of savings came with a 160bp rise in margin, a drop-through of about half. If inflation on the non-commodity cost base falls back, a similar drop-through could happen again.

What would change my view. The February results are the first test. The model implies that the H2-26 gross margin rises about 220bp on a year earlier while the UTOP margin rises about 60bp. A UTOP margin gain well above 60bp would show that Nestlé is keeping more of the savings than I assume.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The structure has little gearing that reaches shareholders: pricing power is cost pass-through with a lag outside pockets (Nespresso, Pro Plan, medical nutrition, EM soluble), truly fixed costs are only 25-30% of sales with an incremental margin of 22-27% that cost inflation absorbs (2%+ RIG adds 10-15bp a year), financial leverage of about 3x does not amplify EPS (no buybacks, 46% of debt refinancing at about 4% against 2.3%), and only about a quarter of the large cost-out reaches the margin. The cost-out scope after 2027 and the advertising-volume and pet-capacity loops keep it above the 25 level; organic growth of 3.6% gives about 5% engine EPS growth (a ratio near 1.4 against the Universe's usual 2), between the Economic strength (48) and Financial forecasts (30) groups.

#6Forecast financials; scope for double digit or higher growth; scope for higher growth/margins than the past over the next four years or so

Conclusion: The forecasts show a real operating recovery of about 5% a year that reported EPS will not display until FY29, with no scope for double-digit growth and margins that only regain their former level by the end of the decade.

The forecasts of record

Three lines where the table departs from the model's printed figure

  • FY26 EPS. The model prints CHF 4.35, because it takes the reported first half on a different definition, with a tax rate lifted by non-deductible losses. On the brokers' basis FY26 EPS is CHF 4.55. The model's EPS growth rates of +1.5% for FY26 and +4.1% for FY27 are artefacts of the different definition.
  • Free cash flow. The model's equity free cash flow, about CHF 10.3bn a year, leaves out restructuring cash and counts associate income that Nestlé does not receive in cash. The table uses the Analyst's cross-check instead.
  • Net debt. The model's year-end net debt (CHF 61.0bn at end-FY26) charges each year's dividend a year early. The table uses the cross-check's debt path instead.

Why EPS stalls while the engine grows: the bridge from FY26 to FY27

Inference

  • Double-digit growth is not on offer. EPS grows about 2.1% a year from FY25 to FY30 (CHF 4.42 to 4.91). A better description of the path is two flat years, then growth of about 3.5% a year once the perimeter stops shrinking.
  • The forecast path is modestly better than the past. On FactSet's adjusted series, EPS fell from CHF 5.10 to 3.94 over FY19 to FY25; on the company's underlying basis it was roughly flat (an unverified figure; end note 5). On either basis, the improvement comes from two sources: a margin that rises 20bp a year where it used to fall, and a franc assumed to cost about 1.5 points a year where it cost about 4.
  • Margins recover to the 2022 to 2024 level only by FY29 to FY30. I hold the margin forecast to about ±30bp in any year, not to the decimal shown.
  • Cash covers the dividend, and no more. Free cash flow after leases covers the dividend about 1.08 times in FY27. Disposals take leverage down in one step in FY27, to about 2.5 times. Leverage then stalls, because the dividend absorbs the cash. The model has only token buybacks: CHF 0.5bn in FY29 and CHF 1.0bn in FY30.

Against consensus. Consensus has reported revenue rising in FY27 and FY28; the model has it falling, and the consensus view cannot survive the shrinking perimeter. Below operating profit, FactSet's consensus implies finance costs falling to about CHF 1.0bn by FY28, while the model holds them at CHF 1.40bn. If FactSet's reading is right, the finance-cost difference is worth about CHF 0.12 a share, or 2.6% of FY28 EPS. However, the company-compiled consensus has CHF 1.46bn for FY27, the model's own figure, so I treat the true gap on finance costs as smaller.

No model input is changed. I tested five candidate changes to the model's inputs and agree with the research that none is worth making: together they move FY27 EPS by only about +0.1% to +0.2% (end note 6).

My leans around the model. I lean towards organic growth a little lower than the model and a first-half 2027 margin a little higher. For FY28 the model is a low-end central estimate: at today's exchange rate FY28 EPS would be about CHF 4.67 to 4.70, and the model sits almost 4% below the lowest broker.

Strongest counter-case. Consensus could be right for the wrong reasons. A flat franc, most of the commodity relief kept and a second savings programme would together take FY28 EPS to about CHF 5.0 to 5.2. I put that outcome at about 25%.

What would change my view. A restated base in February that shows smaller exit effects than I assume; a first-half 2027 margin near 17%; a franc that weakens.

Score: 32, set by the Rater. About 1.9% sits in the lower half of the 0-5% D band: EPS is flat for two years and then grows about 3.5%, against a consensus 5.9% (19th percentile). I place it a little above the band's lower part because the growth is organic, the shortfall is a perimeter cleaned of low-margin units plus an assumed franc drift (about 2.6-3% at today's rate), and the margin rises about 20bp a year where it fell, though only back to the 2022-24 level by FY29-30.

#7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades to company guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative (investors and sell-side) over the coming 6-12 months

Conclusion: Over the next 6 to 12 months, estimates for FY27 and FY28 are more likely to be cut than raised, for mechanical reasons, while guidance is met and opinion stays supportive. The scope for upgrades is poor now and improves only once the base is restated.

What I expect, line by line

Evidence

  • The spread of broker estimates is the tell. Seven houses that have rebuilt their models for Russia sit at CHF 4.55 to 4.66 for FY27: Redburn, Morgan Stanley, Barclays, Bernstein, Santander, Jefferies and one unnamed house. The other twelve sit at CHF 4.69 to 4.92. The median lies in the high group, so as that group rebuilds, the median falls without any new information.
  • The benchmark that Nestlé's results are judged against is higher still. The company-compiled consensus has CHF 4.80 for FY27. Nestlé will collect it again before the February results, and that collection is the first point at which every broker must state a view on Russia.
  • How much of the gap is certain. About three-quarters of the model's FY27 gap to consensus is perimeter arithmetic, and about 40% of the FY28 gap. The rest depends on the franc and on finance costs, which brokers revise slowly. Consensus therefore falls towards the model, but probably not all the way within 18 months.

Two refinements of my own

  • The apparent margin "upgrade" is less clear than it looks. Against FactSet's 16.4% for FY27, the model's 16.6% looks like an upgrade waiting to happen. Against the company-compiled 16.9%, collected before Russia left, it does not. The rebuilt brokers cluster at 16.5% to 16.6%, with Jefferies at 17.0%. I therefore treat the model's margin as in line with where consensus will settle.
  • Expect the Q3 pattern of a volume beat and a price miss to repeat. The model and the company-compiled consensus agree on FY27 organic growth (3.6% and 3.7%) but differ on its mix: the model has RIG of 2.4% and pricing of 1.2%, and the company-compiled consensus has 2.0% and 1.7%. If the model is right, Nestlé beats on volume and misses on price, as in Q3, and the market has rewarded exactly that combination.

The sequence of EPS prints is front-loaded

The half-year prints as a table
Half-yearEPS on a year earlierReported
H2-26about +8%18 February 2027
H1-27about 0%late July 2027
H2-27about −1% to −2%February 2028

The EPS print the market sees gets worse while the business does not. The first-half 2027 margin, which brokers treat as the test, will read about 16.5% against 16.4% a year earlier. Underneath, the gain is about 40bp, hidden by the non-repeat of the pension credit and by Russia's absence.

Inference. Over 6 to 12 months the scope for upgrades lies in opinion, not in EPS: target prices, ratings, the FY26 cash figure and possibly the savings target. Estimates of EPS, revenue and operating profit fall. That order is the wrong way round for a case that depends on upgrades.

February to April 2027 matters most for the same reason. If the company restates a clean base, the mechanical cuts to consensus happen in one burst. After that burst, consensus for FY27 would sit about 1.5% above the model, the bar would be honest, and for the first time in four years the skew on estimates would be roughly balanced.

A difference from the precedents. When Unilever sold its spreads and tea businesses, and when Nestlé sold US confectionery in 2018, buybacks cushioned the earnings dilution. This time the proceeds repay debt, so the dilution lands in EPS in full. For that reason I rely less than the precedents suggest on the pattern that "multiples re-rate before estimates turn".

Does the estimate cycle matter for the shares? So far, no. On 22 October Morgan Stanley cut FY27 EPS by 4% for Russia, and the shares rose on the RIG print. The danger is a weak RIG print arriving together with the re-basing. That combination is most plausible on 18 February, if Q4 RIG is below about 1.5%. Western European volumes began the fourth quarter at −3.2% (Bernstein).

Against the market. The prevailing narrative expects upgrades to follow the volume recovery. I expect one more mechanical leg down in estimates first.

Strongest counter-case. The market may have done the perimeter arithmetic already and simply not written it down. Positioning shows no group of investors set up for bad news. If so, the cuts pass without effect and the next surprise is positive.

What would change my view. I put the chance that FY27 consensus EPS is higher in twelve months at about 15%. It would take a franc 5% weaker (worth about +4% to EPS), a FY27 margin near 17% (about +3%), or a second savings programme with a stated net benefit.

Score: 26, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely met rather than raised (about 60% in line, 15% better, 25% worse for FY27), with the FY27 cash guide likely 10% below consensus; consensus FY27 EPS is about 75-80% likely to fall about 2.5% and FY28 3.5-5.5%, mechanically, as the stale high group of brokers rebuilds for Russia and the exits, a scaled size of about -0.7 times the 3.6% organic growth rate (roughly the 20th percentile), with only FY26 EPS, FY26 cash, a possible second savings programme (35% by February) and a supportive narrative on the plus side. That is the stale-consensus-above-updated-brokers pattern of the 25 level, coherent with the fourth set (32) but lower because cuts are near-certain, between Indutrade and Xvivo.

#8Currently strong momentum in guidance upgrades, sell-side upgrades, narrative (investors and sell-side), share price technical momentum, and the same for key peers

Conclusion: Momentum is strong in price and opinion but weak in estimates and guidance, and about half of the recent strength belongs to the sector, so it is not yet the broad, self-reinforcing momentum of a delivering stock.

Evidence (dashboard readings of 13 to 16 November 2026)

  • Share price. The shares closed at CHF 87.72 on 13 November, at their 52-week high of 87.75 and 10.8% above the 200-day average. They have returned +10.8% over three months and +12.4% over twelve. Relative strength is at the 62nd percentile of the universe, and the dashboard's technical momentum rating is C.
  • Estimates. FY27 EPS revisions are −1% over one and three months, +1% over six and −2% over twelve. EBITDA and sales revisions are slightly negative over every period. The revision score is −1, and the sell-side earnings momentum rating is D.
  • Opinion. Target prices are up 1%. The share of buy ratings is up 8 points, to 44%. The mean target of CHF 88.6 equals the share price.
  • Guidance. Reaffirmed, not raised.
  • Narrative. The narrative has moved from "broken staple" in mid-2025 to "turnaround with volume traction". Jefferies rates the shares Buy with a CHF 94 target, and made Nestlé a franchise pick in October. Morgan Stanley is Underweight with a CHF 76 target. Deutsche Bank, Bernstein, UBS and Redburn are neutral and call the valuation full.
  • Peers. Momentum is worse among the large branded names. On technical and earnings momentum, Danone is rated C and C, Orkla D and F, Lindt F and F, and Associated British Foods C and F. Twelve-month returns are −7.1% for Danone, −29.0% for Lindt and +9.2% for Orkla. Lindt and Reckitt have cut guidance; Unilever and Colgate have raised it.
  • Sector. The dashboard's thematic rating is A. Defensive shares have outperformed the European market by about 8% since mid-2026 (Morgan Stanley), although Redburn notes that defensives' estimate momentum still lags that of cyclicals.

Inference. Momentum is split: price and opinion are strong, estimates and guidance are not. The multiple has done all the work. Over twelve months the shares rose 12% while FY27 EPS estimates fell 2%.

Most of the recent share price move is not Nestlé's own. Over the last six months, the basket of European food producers explains about 47% of the daily variance in Nestlé's share price, against a two-year average of 28%. Nestlé's beta to that basket is 1.26. The basket rose 7.6% and Nestlé 10.1%. Beta times the basket's rise is 9.6%, so only about half a point of Nestlé's six-month gain was its own.

So what. Nestlé's price momentum rests on borrowed support. To continue, it needs either the sector to stay firm or Nestlé's own estimates to turn up, and I expect the estimates to go the wrong way first (#7). With a beta above one, Nestlé is now a geared way to own the food sector, not a refuge inside it: a 10% fall in the basket would imply a fall of about 12% to 13% in Nestlé's shares before any company news.

Against the market. I agree with the market that Nestlé has out-executed its large branded peers over the past year and has earned a re-rating against them. I disagree that the last six months show continuing company-specific momentum; they show a sector move.

Strongest counter-case. Relative momentum is what attracts capital, and Nestlé's relative momentum is the best among the large European food names. The rotation into defensive shares could run further if markets stay nervous.

What would change my view. On the positive side: positive EPS revisions over three months, or the sector's share of Nestlé's price variance falling back while the shares hold their gains. On the negative side: a break below the 200-day moving average.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. One measure negative and one positive gives C: FY27 EPS revisions are -1% over one and three months and EBITDA and sales revisions slightly negative, guidance reaffirmed not raised, against a price at its 52-week high 10.8% above the 200-day, buy ratings up 8 points and a narrative moved to 'turnaround with volume traction'. I place it in the lower-middle of the band because about half the six-month gain is the food sector's (beta 1.26) and estimates are due to fall; peers are weaker but do not move it.

#9Riskiness/simplicity of forecasts/expectations

Conclusion: Nestlé's operations are low-risk and easy to track, but the investment case is not simple. The main risk to the share price is a valuation that rests on consensus earnings due to be cut and on a sector move, with realistic downside of about 15% to 25%.

Simplicity. The business is simple to forecast; the case is not. Organic growth has stayed within 3.5% to 4.0% in each of the last four quarters, and for FY27 it should fall between about 2.9% and 4.0%. Yet reported EPS depends on four exits, a currency, a commodity cycle, a round of retailer negotiations and one unguided cost line, net savings.

The cone of outcomes. For FY27 I put EPS at CHF 4.32 to 4.74 around a central CHF 4.53, a range of about ±4.6%. The franc accounts for about three-quarters of that variance; without the franc the range is about ±2.4%. The FY28 cone is more than twice as wide, at CHF 4.1 to 5.2.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic. All figures use the model's FY27 base unless stated: revenue of CHF 88.2bn, a tax rate of 22% on operating items and 2,572m shares. On that base, 10bp of margin is CHF 88m of UTOP, CHF 69m after tax, CHF 0.027 a share, or 0.6% of EPS.

Judgement 1: volume holds near 2%. Suppose RIG is one point lower than the model's 2.4%.

  • Sales: 1% of CHF 88.2bn is CHF 0.88bn less.
  • UTOP: at an incremental margin of 22% to 27%, CHF 0.19bn to 0.24bn less, about 1.5% of UTOP and about 10bp of margin.
  • EPS: CHF 0.15bn to 0.19bn less after tax, or CHF 0.06 to 0.07 a share, about 1.4%.
  • Free cash flow: about CHF 0.15bn to 0.19bn less, about 2%.
  • The larger effect of weaker volume is on the multiple. One turn on two-year-forward EPS of CHF 4.56 is CHF 4.56 a share, or 5.2% of the price. Deutsche Bank's reading is that Nestlé has needed RIG above 2% to hold a multiple above its median. A point of RIG is therefore worth about 1.4% in earnings and plausibly a turn or more in valuation.

Judgement 2: Nestlé keeps about half of the coffee and cocoa relief, and costs do not turn up before 2028. The model has about 70bp of relief reaching the FY27 accounts, with half kept (+35bp), and 15bp given back in FY28.

  • If Nestlé keeps a quarter of the relief, not half: 17.5bp less margin is CHF 0.15bn of UTOP, CHF 0.12bn after tax and CHF 0.047 a share, or −1.0% of FY27 EPS. If it keeps three-quarters, the effect is +1.0%.
  • Revenue moves more than profit, because price given back lowers sales while the cost base has also fallen. Organic growth and the margin therefore tend to miss in opposite directions, which narrows the EPS cone.
  • If costs turn up early and the FY28 give-back is 50bp, not 15bp: the extra 35bp on FY28 revenue of CHF 87.6bn is CHF 0.31bn of UTOP, CHF 0.24bn after tax and CHF 0.093 a share, or −2.0% of FY28 EPS. The 2025 cost episode cost 110bp of gross margin before pricing caught up.

Judgement 3: the franc drifts 1.0% and then 1.5% a year stronger. Suppose the average rate is 5% stronger than assumed.

  • Sales: CHF 4.4bn less.
  • UTOP: translation alone removes about CHF 0.73bn. A further 10bp to 15bp of margin, about CHF 0.11bn, is lost because Swiss-based costs do not shrink.
  • EPS: the rule of thumb used by the company and the brokers is about 4%, or CHF 0.18 a share. Plain translation of UTOP alone gives CHF 0.57bn after tax, or 4.9% of EPS, before any offset from interest paid in other currencies. I therefore treat 4% as a floor.
  • Dividend cover: free cash flow after leases of CHF 8.78bn is nearly all earned abroad, while the dividend paid in 2027 (CHF 3.15 on 2,572m shares, or CHF 8.10bn) is fixed in francs. Cover of 1.08 times falls to about 1.03 times with a franc 5% stronger, and to 1.0 times with a franc 8% stronger. This is the link between the franc and the debate about the dividend.
  • In the other direction, if the franc simply stays at today's rate, FY27 EPS is about CHF 4.57, FY28 about CHF 4.67 to 4.70 and FY29 about CHF 4.91.

Judgement 4: a quarter of the savings reaches the margin. The model has about CHF 0.7bn of the CHF 3.0bn showing in the margin by FY28. Suppose the truth is CHF 0.25bn more or less, a drop-through of about a third or about 15%.

  • Margin: CHF 0.25bn on FY28 revenue of CHF 87.6bn is 29bp, giving a margin of 17.1% or 16.5% against the model's 16.8%.
  • EPS: CHF 0.195bn after tax, or CHF 0.076 a share, ±1.7% of FY28 EPS.
  • A second savings programme worth 15bp to 20bp of margin a year from FY28 would add about CHF 0.046 a share, or about 1% of EPS a year.

Judgement 5: the market pays up through a downgrade cycle. The model applies 20.17 times to two-year-forward EPS of CHF 4.76 at end-2027. Each turn of multiple is worth CHF 4.76 a share, or 5.4% of today's price.

Reading the five judgements together. Judgements 1 to 4 each move EPS by 1% to 4%. Judgement 5 moves the share price by about 5% for each turn of multiple. The share price risk is therefore mostly a valuation risk, and the valuation depends mostly on RIG and on the sector. That is why a forecast can be right on every operating line while the shares still disappoint.

Fragilities and required assumptions. The case needs no buyback, no acquisition, no real price increase and no margin above 17% before FY29. The one new strength it does need is organisational: removing 6% of the workforce without harm to sales.

Sudden risks: prevalence and size

  • A second food-safety event. The Q1-26 recall cost about CHF 200m to 270m of sales and 90bp of that quarter's growth. A repeat would hit trust in the nutrition business hardest.
  • A jump in the franc of 10% or more in a risk-off market would cut EPS by about 8% or more.
  • Coordinated delistings by a European buying alliance. The dispute between Edeka and Mars ran for about 18 months.
  • Withdrawal of supplier finance. Reverse factoring is CHF 6.2bn, about 7% of sales. Losing it would mean a multi-billion cash outflow and no dividend cover.
  • A sector rotation. A rotation out of staples is the most likely of the five risks, and is unrelated to Nestlé's own results.

Each of the first four risks is unlikely within 18 months. All four share one mechanism: each would force Nestlé back towards price increases or cost cuts that undo the volume strategy.

Predictability and trackability are good. Nestlé reports RIG and pricing every quarter by zone and category. Commodity futures, scanner data and the franc can be read daily or monthly. The gaps are net savings, commodity cover and the outcome of retailer talks, none of which Nestlé discloses.

Sector and cyclicality, with precedents. Demand is barely cyclical. The cycles that matter are commodities, the franc and the sector's rating against bond yields.

  • Staples turnarounds take two to four years. Procter & Gamble took about 24 months to go from 18.5 times to 25.5 times earnings once growth turned. Danone needed nine consecutive quarters of positive volume to close its valuation discount.
  • Setbacks are punished fast. Nestlé fell 8% in five days after its Q2-25 results. Reckitt's re-rating was undone by one manufacturing problem.
  • The failure case is Kraft Heinz. Cost cuts without reinvestment took its multiple to 10.8 times.

How far could the shares fall? At the trough multiple of 14.9 times on today's two-year-forward EPS, the shares would be about CHF 74 on consensus earnings (−16%) and about CHF 68 on ours (−23%).

Against the market. The market treats Nestlé as low-risk because its operations are steady. I agree about the operations, but I think the market underrates the valuation risk: the share price rests on consensus earnings that are due to fall, and on a sector move.

Strongest counter-case. A dividend yield of 3.6%, covered and raised for 66 years, with the L'Oréal stake behind it, limits the downside more than a trough multiple suggests.

What would change my view. A restated base and settled European terms would remove two of the five moving parts by April 2027.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Operations are barely cyclical and trackable, and the memo's FY27 EPS cone is narrow (CHF 4.32-4.74, about +/-4.6%, three-quarters of it the franc), but the FY28 cone more than doubles (CHF 4.1-5.2), reported EPS rests on four exits, a currency, a commodity cycle, retailer talks and unguided net savings, leverage is about 3x (75th percentile, though 80% fixed), CHF 6.2bn of supplier finance is a tail risk, and the share price risk is a multiple resting on consensus due to fall and a sector beta of 1.26 (realistic downside 15-25%). Coherent with the Risks groups (52, 55): just below Banca Generali's single-sensitivity case and above NKT's concentrated execution risk.

#10An assessment of where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Nestlé is early in turning up, with operations and the share price ahead of estimates that have one more leg down, and the test of whether the thesis broadens falls between February and July 2027.

Evidence by dimension

  • Operations: turning up. Volume is positive in all zones, share loss is slowing and savings are ahead of plan. Profit has not yet inflected: once the pension credit is removed, the H1-26 margin was lower than a year earlier.
  • Share price and narrative: turning up, on volume alone. The shares are about 29% above their month-end low of July 2025 and at a 52-week high.
  • Estimates: still bottoming. Revisions are slightly negative, with one more mechanical leg down to come.
  • Guidance: stable. Met and defended, not raised.
  • Risk factors. Falling for the fundamentals, rising for the valuation.

Inference. The stock is early in the "turning up" phase, which matches the dashboard's starting phase of Turning/Inflecting. It is not yet in "thesis broadening", because broadening needs estimates to rise and the evidence to spread from volume to margin and cash. It is not "stalling", because the engine is improving.

The combination is unusual. Normally a stock that is turning up has rising estimates behind the price. Here the price has turned ahead of estimates that are still to fall, for reasons that have nothing to do with trading.

So what. A stock in the "turning up" phase earns a multiple in the lower part of its range until the forecasts firm (#11). The next phase is dated:

  • Broadening needs a clean base (February to April 2027), a first-half margin that reads well once adjusted (July 2027), and a signal on savings or capital returns (by February 2028).
  • Stalling would show as RIG below 1.5%, cuts to advertising, or delistings.

Against the market. Jefferies writes as if the thesis is already broadening; Morgan Stanley writes as if it will stall. I sit between them: turning up, with the test of broadening about six to nine months away.

Strongest counter-case. The market may move the stock on to the next phase on volume alone, as it did in 2026, and treat the estimate cuts as housekeeping.

What would change my view. Two more quarters of RIG at 2% or better without weather help would make me call the stock late in its turn. A Q4 RIG below 1.5% would make me call it at risk of stalling.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's early Turning up rather than the computed Bottoming for operations and the share price (volume positive in all zones, savings ahead, shares 29% off the 2025 low at a 52-week high), but estimates are still bottoming with one more mechanical leg down and profit has not inflected, so the price has turned ahead of forecasts and the volume good news is largely known. That is a less attractive point than a confirmed turn: between Greggs (Bottoming/early Turning) and Solid State (Bottoming moving to Turning), nearer Greggs.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion: The guideline multiple of 20.17 times is a fair ceiling for the next phase but generous for this one. I would plan on about 18.5 to 19.5 times our earnings, which makes the shares about fairly valued today.

The guideline. The dashboard sets the fair multiple for a stock in the Turning/Inflecting phase at 20.18 times two-year-forward earnings, the 60th percentile of Nestlé's own ten-year history. The model uses 20.17 times, reached at its 18-month column.

Where the multiple stands today depends on whose earnings are used. There are three readings.

  • 17.6 times on consensus earnings (FactSet, 13 November).
  • 17.1 times on the dashboard's Phases page (18 November), which uses a later date and possibly a lower price than the model.
  • 19.3 times on the model's earnings.

The guideline is 18% above the dashboard's reading but only 4.5% above the multiple on our earnings. The same guideline multiple is therefore worth about CHF 101 a share on consensus earnings today and about CHF 92 on ours.

The history of the multiple

PeriodMedianOther markers
Ten years19.5x10th percentile 16.3x; 35th percentile 18.5x; 75th percentile 21.4x
Five years17.7xMiddle half 16.5x to 19.8x; range 14.9x to 24.9x
Last two years16.4xNo month has ended at or above 20x since April 2023

My view. The guideline is at the generous end for this stock in this phase. I would use it as a ceiling for the next 12 to 18 months and centre my own expectation at about 18.5 to 19.5 times our earnings. On that view the shares are fairly valued today, for five reasons:

  1. The ten-year distribution is dominated by a different company. From mid-2019 to early 2023 the multiple was mostly at or above 20 times. Nestlé was then retiring about 2% of its shares a year, leverage was rising from a low base and bond yields were low. None of those conditions holds now.
  2. The guideline's own logic argues for a lower multiple. A stock that is turning up, with forecasts still uncertain, belongs in the lower part of its range, yet the 60th percentile of ten years is above the 75th percentile of the last five.
  3. The growth does not support the guideline. The model has EPS flat for two years and growing about 3.5% a year after. On my own rough arithmetic, a payout of about 70%, long-run growth of about 3% and a required return of 6.5% to 7% support a multiple of about 18 to 20 times, not more.
  4. The headline multiple flatters. Excluding the L'Oréal stake, the multiple on the core business is about one turn lower.
  5. Brokers attach conditions to any multiple above the median. Jefferies' 20 times is its re-rating case. Deutsche Bank requires sustained RIG above 2%. Morgan Stanley's bear case uses about 14 times.

What would justify the guideline. Estimates that have stopped falling; RIG held at 2% or better through 2027; a first-half margin that reads well; and leverage near 2.5 times with a word on buybacks. With those conditions in place, 20 times is reasonable. They describe the next phase, however, not this one.

Against the market. The market believes it is paying a mid-range multiple with room to re-rate. I believe it is paying close to a full multiple on earnings that have not yet been re-based.

Strongest counter-case. Swiss interest rates are at zero. A dividend yield of 3.6% from a franc-denominated staple is scarce, and that scarcity could hold the multiple above what the growth alone supports.

What would change my view. Consensus settling at or above the model's numbers would remove my main objection, because the multiple investors see and the multiple on our earnings would then be the same.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. On the figures this is cheap on one and neutral on the other (B), but step 2 moves it to C: the cheapness rests on consensus earnings the memo shows are due to fall 4-9% for arithmetic reasons, the ten-year range was built in a buyback, low-yield regime, and a Turning stock belongs low in its range, so on re-based earnings both readings are neutral. Placed in the upper half of C because the multiple on our earnings still sits a little below the ten-year median and below the 20.17x guideline, though above the five-year median.

#12Total shareholder return, via dupont framework

Conclusion: The model's return of +16.2% over 18 months and +24.9% over three years is mostly dividend plus a back-loaded earnings step. I would plan on about +7% to +12% over 18 months, because the re-rating part is the least secure.

The model's return at the guideline fair multiple

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedDividendsMultipleEarningsValue per share
18-month column, to 31 December 2027+16.2%+14.3%+7.2%+4.5%+4.3%CHF 102.27
Three-year column, to 30 June 2029+24.9%+8.8%+10.9%+4.5%+9.1%CHF 109.88

What drives each part of the return

  • Dividends (+7.2%, then +10.9%).
    • The first column includes two payments, CHF 3.15 and CHF 3.20; the second adds a third, of CHF 3.25.
    • Dividends are the most dependable part of the return. Cover is thin, at about 1.08 times, but Nestlé has held or raised its dividend for 66 years.
    • One caution on timing: the CHF 3.20 is paid in April 2028, after the first column's date. Up to 31 December 2027 only one payment is received, and the return is about +12.6%. The +16.2% is therefore best read as a return to about May 2028.
  • Earnings (+4.3%, then +9.1%).
    • The earnings part is the change in two-year-forward EPS, from about CHF 4.56 today to CHF 4.76 (FY29) at end-2027 and about CHF 4.97 by mid-2029.
    • The first step does not come from growth in the next two years, which is nil. It comes from the forward window rolling past the perimeter shrinkage into FY29, the first clean year.
    • The earnings part is therefore back-loaded, and it depends on the engine still growing about 4% to 5% underneath in FY29.
  • The multiple (+4.5% in both columns).
    • The multiple part is the move from 19.3 times to 20.17 times on our earnings, taken once.
    • The multiple is the least dependable part (#11). In terms the market sees, it requires the multiple on consensus earnings to rise from 17.6 times to about 20 times while consensus EPS falls 8% to 9%.

The return is a yield-plus-modest-growth return, not a growth or recovery return. About 44% of the return is dividend over both horizons. Over three years, the annualised return of 8.8% comprises about 3.7 points of yield, about 3.4 of earnings and about 1.7 of re-rating.

Sensitivity to the multiple. The grid in #9 (judgement 5) gives the 18-month return at other multiples: about +12% if the market keeps today's multiple on our earnings, about +7% at 18.5 times, about +2% at today's screen multiple of 17.6 times, and about −12% at the 2025 trough. Each turn of multiple is worth 5.4 points of return, and each 1% of EPS about 1 point.

Two adjustments Richard may want to make

  • The franc. The return is in francs. The model builds about 4% of cumulative franc strength into FY27 to FY29 sales, which costs about CHF 0.15 of FY29 EPS. A holder who measures returns in another currency gets most of that back through the currency of the shares if the franc does strengthen; if it does not, EPS is higher. Either way, I estimate that such a holder's return is roughly 2 to 3 points better than the franc figure by the first column.
  • The entry price. On my preferred multiple of about 19 times, the price at end-2027 is about CHF 90. An 18-month return of 15% including dividends would then need an entry price of about CHF 84: CHF 90 plus CHF 6.35 of dividends, divided by 1.15. This arithmetic is my own.

Against the market. Target prices cluster around today's price, which implies a return of about the dividend. The guideline return is higher than the market's. My planned return lies between the two, nearer the market's.

Strongest counter-case. If the market looks through the re-basing, as it has so far, and RIG holds, a multiple of 20 times on FY29 earnings is plausible by 2028, and the return is as the model shows.

What would change my view. A lower entry price; consensus re-based to the model's level with the shares holding; or a franc that weakens.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The memo's own weighting centres the 18-month return at about +9.5%, just inside D (about 48 on the scale), because the +16.2% needs a re-rating to 20.17x through a downgrade cycle and includes a dividend paid in April 2028; it is mostly dividend (7.2 points) with a back-loaded earnings step. I move it down two points for the fat lower tail (about -12% at the 2025 trough multiple, sector beta 1.26); the three-year check at the guideline multiple is supportive only if the re-rating comes.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Is the skew unusually positive? Not today. Fundamental outcomes are steady and slightly favourable. The probability of upgrades to estimates over the next six to twelve months is low, and the probability of cuts is high. The reasons for the cuts are mechanical and benign in kind, but they run the wrong way for an approach that looks for positive skew.

The business. Nestlé is a high-margin, cash-generative, barely cyclical franchise with a protected core in petcare, coffee and nutrition and a contested middle. It lost its way from 2022 to 2025 through price-led growth, poor acquisitions and rising leverage. New leadership is fixing the operating problems quickly and credibly: volume has turned, the savings are real and the portfolio is being cleaned.

The investment case. The operating recovery is worth about 5% a year in EPS. For two years the wrapper hides that recovery: Russia, the exits, a drifting franc, flat finance costs and no buybacks. Consensus has not yet taken the wrapper in, so estimates must fall by about 2.5% to 5% in the first half of 2027. On the model's earnings the shares are on 19.3 times, close to a full multiple. The return on offer is the dividend plus a modest, back-loaded earnings step, with re-rating as an uncertain extra.

What would make the skew positive. Three dated steps would. First, the restated base and re-collected consensus of February to April 2027, which should clear the mechanical cuts in one burst. Second, a first-half 2027 margin that confirms the engine. Third, a second savings programme or a first word on capital returns. A lower entry price would do the same work faster. Until then, Nestlé is a well-run turnaround to follow closely, with a clear watch-list and known dates.

Practical next steps. Read the aide-mémoire and the re-collected consensus about three weeks before 18 February. On the day, check four numbers in this order: Q4 RIG (1.8% or better supports the case; below 1.5% does not), the H2-26 gross margin (about 46.5% or better), the advertising ratio (9% of sales or better) and the scope statement.

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 46, set by the Rater. The input forces net only mildly positive (strong, self-funded internal change at 64 against a modest external headwind at 45), and they do not reach profits within the horizon: the engine grows EPS about 5% but the shrinking perimeter and franc hold forecast EPS flat for two years and to about 1.9% a year to FY30 (D, 32), well below the Universe's typical growth. So the change that reaches profits is slightly below no material net change, a mild net negative in the mid-40s.

Foundations' Robustness: 66, set by the Rater. Quality at 61 rests on a protected, barely cyclical core of top-two positions with stable gross margins, cash generation and very predictable 2-4% organic growth, which Richard's CVS ruling shows lifts robustness above what ordinary returns suggest; it is held well short of 75 by concentrated retailers and no real pricing power, years of share loss, the highest leverage in its peer set, poor capital allocation and a delivery record (45) of a guidance cut and estimates falling.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 64, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits 'CfC Clearing in an HQ low-cyclicality business': the cause for concern (price-led volume loss, leadership churn) is clearing with volume turned and a reset under way in a good-quality, barely cyclical franchise, a better quality than Richard's CVS 65-75 case. The fit is loosened by today's problems (the reversion in EPS delayed to FY29 by the shrinking perimeter, share loss not yet stopped, staff cuts and the formula recall), while the multiple's cheapness only on consensus is a price matter judged elsewhere and does not count here.

Case Riskiness: 57, set by the Rater. Riskiness at 58: boring operations with paper-cut operating risks and a narrow FY27 cone, but a case with many moving parts, a currency driving three-quarters of the EPS variance, about 3x leverage, and a share price resting on consensus due to be cut, a mid-range multiple on re-based earnings and a 1.26 sector beta. That keeps it in the upper 50s, well below Richard's CVS 80-85 (conservative guidance, low multiple) and close to his Arteche 60 (multiple and sector-flow risk on a simple operating case).

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
